card_summary: The push for IP-based broadcast infrastructure continues, with vendors demonstrating interoperability across ST 2110 and NDI. While ST 2110 remains the bedrock for professional, uncompressed transport requiring strict Genlock and frame accuracy, NDI's growing adoption signals a pragmatic acceptance of compressed, lower-latency IP workflows for less critical paths or remote contribution. This bifurcation isn't about one winning; it's about fitting the right tool to the job, from core infrastructure to flexible studio feeds. For engineering teams, the real challenge is managing this growing diversity of protocols. Ensuring consistent signal integrity and reliable Genlock across disparate IP streams, whether ST 2110 or NDI, demands robust network design and meticulous monitoring. The trade-off is complexity; while offering flexibility, it necessitates deeper expertise in network protocols and synchronization beyond traditional SDI.
body_html:
Why IP Media Transport is Forcing a Re-evaluation of Live Production Infrastructure

The pressure to reduce latency and improve signal integrity in live broadcast environments is intensifying. As facilities move away from SDI matrices and towards IP-based infrastructures, the need for robust, reliable, and frame-accurate signal transport becomes paramount. This shift demands a critical look at how we manage and move uncompressed and lightly compressed media signals within the studio and beyond.

What This Development Actually Means

Studio Network Solutions (SNS) has announced their presence at the FORTÉ LIVE event in Indianapolis, showcasing their solutions for media infrastructure. This presence signals a continued industry focus on integrated storage and networking for live production environments, particularly those leveraging IP transport. The underlying trend is the convergence of IT and broadcast infrastructure, pushing for more flexible and scalable workflows that can handle the demands of modern live broadcasting.

Why It Matters for Broadcast Operations

The move towards IP, driven by standards like SMPTE ST 2110, presents both opportunities and challenges for broadcast engineers. While it promises greater flexibility and reduced cabling complexity, it also introduces new considerations around network design, signal synchronization, and the management of IP streams. Vendors like Evertz with their IP gateways and routing solutions, and Riedel with their MediorNet systems, are key players in this transition, offering hardware that bridges the gap between traditional SDI and IP workflows. For engineering teams, this means a significant investment in training and new hardware, but also the potential for OpEx savings by consolidating infrastructure and enabling remote production capabilities. The ability to seamlessly integrate JPEG XS or uncompressed ST 2110 streams into existing workflows, while maintaining Genlock and frame accuracy, is no longer a luxury but a necessity. This necessitates careful planning around network segmentation, Quality of Service (QoS) implementation, and the adoption of discovery and control protocols like NMOS.

Impact by Stakeholder

  • Regional and national broadcasters: Will need to budget for significant network upgrades and potentially new IP-enabled studio equipment. The reduction in physical cabling and the ability to route signals more dynamically can eliminate the need for expensive SDI matrix expansions and simplify remote contribution links, potentially lowering transmission costs compared to dedicated fiber or satellite.
  • OTT and streaming platforms: While not directly involved in live signal transport within the studio, these platforms will benefit from more efficiently produced and lower-latency source feeds. This can translate to improved viewer experience and potentially reduced encoding costs if the incoming feeds are cleaner and more consistent. The ability to ingest high-quality, low-latency feeds via SRT or ST 2110 can simplify origin server operations.
  • Post-production and MAM teams: Will see improved ingest workflows if live production feeds can be directly captured into their MAM systems via IP. This reduces the need for intermediate SDI capture hardware and streamlines the path from live event to archive and edit. The consistency of ST 2110 streams, with their inherent metadata, can also improve content indexing and searchability within MAM platforms.

Deep Insight: The Broader Industry Shift

We are witnessing a fundamental re-architecture of the broadcast plant, moving from a hardware-centric, signal-path-defined model to a software-defined, IP-centric paradigm. This isn't just about replacing SDI cables with Ethernet; it's about embracing IT principles for media transport and processing. The industry is moving away from proprietary SDI routing matrices and dedicated hardware encoders/decoders towards flexible, software-based solutions that can run on commodity IT hardware or in cloud environments. While NDI offers a more accessible IP solution for certain applications, ST 2110 remains the standard for professional, uncompressed, frame-accurate transport in high-stakes live broadcast. The vendors who will struggle are those clinging to legacy SDI-only architectures without a clear IP migration strategy. The real risk is not the technology itself, but the operational and training gap that must be bridged to effectively manage these new IP-based systems. By 2027, we expect to see a significant majority of new studio builds and major renovations defaulting to ST 2110 infrastructure, with legacy SDI relegated to niche applications or specific contribution links.
